article.plain_text:
In a National Institutes of Health (NIH)-funded study, scientists developed a new method of breaking down environmental contaminants and applied it to polyfluoroalkyl and perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) chemicals, converting them into harmless byproducts. They successfully used this approach to eliminate these contaminants in water, indicating the technique may be a potentially safer and low-energy alternative to leading methods of PFAS removal.
Synthetic PFAS chemicals persist throughout the environment and in our bodies. Most natural processes are incapable of degrading them thanks to their carbon-fluorine bonds, one of the strongest chemical bonds that can exist between two atoms.
Due to their durability, most means of destroying these chemicals rely on creating extreme conditions, such as high heat and pressure or harsh acidity. Other methods can filter PFAS out, but do not ultimately destroy the molecules.
The new strategy, which entails adding either platinum or palladium nanoparticles to contaminated water and then shining low-intensity UV light, can be performed under ambient conditions. In this process, light initiates a chemical reaction between the nanoparticles, PFAS, and water, severing the troublesome chemical bonds. Fluorine atoms are released into water as fluoride ions — the same chemical in toothpaste — and replaced with hydrogen.
The researchers, from Yale University, New Haven, Connecticut, demonstrated that their method eliminated nearly 100% of the two most studied subgroups of PFAS, which they introduced into highly purified water.
In the future, they intend to target more synthetic contaminants such as 1,4-dioxane and other volatile organic compounds and investigate alternative nanomaterial substrates to potentially further boost cost-efficacy. And further down the line, they aim to test the approach in samples that more closely mimic real contaminated water.
Reference: Ozce Durak, Seung Soo S. Lee, et al. Plasmon-Enhanced Reductive Defluorination of PFAS in Water Under Ambient Conditions. Nature Water. 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s44221-026-00690-1
